text: According to Genesis Chapter 1, what did God create on the fourth day?
options: The sun, moon, and stars
Sea creatures and birds
Land animals and mankind
Light and darkness
explanation: On Day 4, God created the heavenly bodies—the sun, moon, and stars—to divide day from night and to serve as signs for seasons, days, and years (Genesis 1:14–19).

text: In the second creation account (Genesis 2), man was formed from:
options: The dust of the ground
The word of God's mouth only
Water and clay
The light of the sun
explanation: Genesis 2:7 states that the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, making him a living soul.

text: The primary temptation presented by the serpent to Eve in the Garden of Eden was that:
options: They would not die, but their eyes would be opened and they would be like God, knowing good and evil.
They would rule over all animals if they ate the fruit.
God would abandon them if they did not eat the fruit.
They would live forever in paradise.
explanation: The serpent deceived Eve by directly contradicting God's warning ("You will not surely die") and appealing to pride and wisdom (Genesis 3:4–5).

text: What immediate consequence did Adam and Eve experience after eating the forbidden fruit?
options: They realized they were naked and hid from God.
They were immediately struck dead physically.
They built an altar to ask for forgiveness.
Cain was born immediately.
explanation: Upon eating the fruit, their eyes were opened, they realized their nakedness, sewed fig leaves together, and hid from God's presence among the trees (Genesis 3:7–8).

text: Why did God accept Abel's offering but reject Cain's offering?
options: Abel offered the firstborn of his flock with faith and reverence, while Cain's heart and offering lacked faith.
God preferred meat offerings over agricultural produce.
Cain brought stolen crops from his neighbor's field.
Abel was older than Cain.
explanation: Genesis 4:4–5 and Hebrews 11:4 highlight that Abel offered by faith a more acceptable sacrifice, whereas Cain's offering lacked proper devotion and a righteous heart.

text: God's sign of the covenant made with Noah never to destroy the earth again with a flood was the:
options: Rainbow
Circumcision
Burning Bush
Pillar of Fire
explanation: Genesis 9:12–17 records that God placed His bow in the clouds as a token of the everlasting covenant between Him and every living creature.

text: In Abraham's call (Genesis 12), God instructed him to leave his country, relatives, and father's house to go to:
options: A land that God would show him (Canaan)
The city of Babylon
The land of Egypt
The wilderness of Sinai
explanation: Abraham was called out of Haran in faith to travel to an undisclosed land that God promised to reveal to him (Genesis 12:1–3).

text: What was the physical sign of the covenant God established with Abraham and his descendants?
options: Circumcision of every male child on the eighth day
Offering a ram every morning
Wearing special priestly garments
Keeping the Sabbath day holy
explanation: Genesis 17:10–14 specifies circumcision as the perpetual physical token of the covenant between God and Abraham's lineage.

text: Abraham demonstrated supreme faith and obedience when God commanded him to:
options: Sacrifice his only son, Isaac, on Mount Moriah.
Send away his wife Sarah into the desert.
Attack the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah alone.
Build an ark for his family.
explanation: God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac as a burnt offering; Abraham obeyed in faith until God stopped him and provided a ram (Genesis 22).

text: Jacob obtained the birthright and blessing intended for his elder brother Esau by:
options: Purchasing the birthright for a bowl of stew and disguising himself to deceive his father Isaac.
Defeating Esau in a physical wrestling match.
Receiving a direct decree from the elders of the land.
Claiming it after Esau died young.
explanation: Jacob bought Esau's birthright for stew (Genesis 25:29–34) and later used goat skins and Esau's garments to receive Isaac's patriarchal blessing (Genesis 27).

text: Where did Jacob wrestle with a divine being and receive the new name "Israel"?
options: Peniel (Jabbok stream)
Bethel
Hebron
Mount Sinai
explanation: At Peniel, Jacob wrestled with God/an angel until daybreak, where his name was changed from Jacob to Israel because he strived with God and men and prevailed (Genesis 32:24–30).

text: Joseph was sold into slavery in Egypt by his brothers primarily because:
options: They envied him due to his father's special love for him and his prophetic dreams.
Joseph stole his brothers' livestock.
Joseph refused to work in the family fields.
Their father Jacob commanded them to send Joseph away.
explanation: Joseph's brothers hated him for his coat of many colors and his dreams predicting their bow to him (Genesis 37:3–11).

text: Joseph rose to the position of prime minister (governor) in Egypt because he:
options: Interpreted Pharaoh's dreams predicting seven years of plenty and seven years of famine.
Led Pharaoh's army to victory against foreign invaders.
Married Pharaoh's eldest daughter.
Organized a successful rebellion against Potiphar.
explanation: God gave Joseph the interpretation of Pharaoh's dreams regarding the coming famine, leading Pharaoh to appoint him over all Egypt to manage food reserves (Genesis 41).

text: When Joseph revealed his identity to his brothers in Egypt, he demonstrated reconciliation by stating that:
options: God sent him ahead of them to preserve life, turning their evil intent into good.
They must pay back all the money they received for selling him.
They must leave their father Jacob behind in Canaan.
He would imprison them as punishment.
explanation: Joseph forgave his brothers, recognizing God's sovereign purpose in using his trials to save many people from starvation (Genesis 45:5–8; 50:20).

text: God revealed His divine name to Moses at the burning bush in Mount Horeb as:
options: I AM WHO I AM (Yahweh)
El Shaddai
Jehovah Jireh
Adonai
explanation: When Moses asked God His name at the burning bush, God answered, "I AM WHO I AM," commissioning him to deliver Israel from Egypt (Exodus 3:13–14).

text: The final plague that compelled Pharaoh to release the Israelites from Egypt was the:
options: Death of the firstborn of humans and livestock in Egypt
Plague of locusts devouring all crops
Turning of the Nile River into blood
Three days of absolute darkness
explanation: The tenth plague struck down all the firstborn in Egypt, prompting Pharaoh to urgently command the Israelites to leave (Exodus 12:29–32).

text: During the Passover meal, the Israelites were instructed to smear the blood of an unblemished lamb on their:
options: Doorposts and lintels of their houses
Altars and garments
Foreheads and hands
Storage vessels and wells
explanation: The blood on the doorposts served as a sign for the Lord to pass over those homes when striking the Egyptian firstborn (Exodus 12:7, 13).

text: How did the Lord guide the Israelites in the wilderness during their journey out of Egypt?
options: By a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night
By sending angels visibly at every junction
By an iron compass given to Moses
By a flock of white doves flying ahead
explanation: Exodus 13:21–22 records that the Lord went before them in a pillar of cloud by day to lead the way and a pillar of fire by night to give light.

text: At the Red Sea, when the Egyptians pursued Israel, Moses stretched out his hand over the sea, and the Lord divided the waters by:
options: A strong east wind blowing all night
A sudden earthquake
Heavy rainfall and lightning
An immediate eclipse
explanation: Moses stretched out his hand, and the Lord drove the sea back by a strong east wind all night, turning the sea into dry land (Exodus 14:21).

text: In the wilderness of Sin, when Israel complained of hunger, God provided them with:
options: Manna in the morning and quail in the evening
Bread from local merchants and wild honey
Figs and olives from the palm trees
Wheat flour dropping from the sky
explanation: Exodus 16 records that God provided meat (quail) in the evening and bread from heaven (manna) in the morning to feed the wandering nation.

text: Where did Moses receive the Ten Commandments written on tables of stone by the finger of God?
options: Mount Sinai (Horeb)
Mount Nebo
Mount Carmel
Mount Gerizim
explanation: God summoned Moses to the top of Mount Sinai, where He gave him the Law and the two stone tablets of the covenant (Exodus 19–20; 31:18).

text: Which commandment carries a specific promise of long life for those who observe it?
options: Honor your father and your mother.
Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
You shall not steal.
You shall have no other gods before me.
explanation: Exodus 20:12 states: "Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long upon the land which the Lord your God gives you."

text: While Moses was on Mount Sinai for forty days, Aaron made a golden calf for Israel to worship because:
options: The people became impatient and demanded visible gods to lead them.
The Pharaoh sent soldiers to force them back into idolatry.
Joshua advised Aaron to test the people's loyalty.
They lacked food and water in the camp.
explanation: Seeing that Moses delayed coming down from the mountain, the people gathered around Aaron and asked for gods to go before them (Exodus 32:1–4).

text: Who succeeded Moses as the leader of Israel to lead them into the Promised Land of Canaan?
options: Joshua, son of Nun
Caleb, son of Jephunneh
Eleazar the priest
Gershom, son of Moses
explanation: God appointed Joshua as Moses' successor, charging him to be strong and courageous as he led Israel across the Jordan (Numbers 27:18–23; Joshua 1).

text: The miraculous event that marked Israel's entry into Canaan under Joshua's leadership was the:
options: Parting of the waters of the Jordan River when the priests carrying the Ark stepped in
Sudden destruction of Mount Seir by earthquake
Eruption of fire from the altar at Gilgal
Falling of manna inside Jericho's walls
explanation: When the feet of the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant touched the edge of the Jordan River, the waters upstream stopped, allowing Israel to cross on dry ground (Joshua 3).

text: How did the fortress walls of Jericho fall according to Joshua Chapter 6?
options: Israel marched around the city for seven days, blew trumpets, shouted, and the walls collapsed.
Joshua's army used battering rams to break down the main gates.
An army of angels set fire to the city walls at midnight.
Rahab opened the gates from the inside for Joshua's spies.
explanation: Following God's command, Israel marched around Jericho once a day for six days, and seven times on the seventh day. Upon blowing the trumpets and shouting, the walls fell flat (Joshua 6).

text: Deborah was unique among the Judges of Israel because she was:
options: A prophetess and the only female judge who led Israel to victory over Sisera.
The mother of King Saul.
A high priestess in the Tabernacle at Shiloh.
The leader who destroyed the temple of Dagon.
explanation: Judges 4 describes Deborah as a prophetess and judge who summoned Barak to fight against Jabin's army commander, Sisera.

text: Gideon reduced his army from 32,000 men down to 300 before fighting the Midianites by selecting those who:
options: Lapped water from their hands like a dog while remaining alert
Knelt down directly on their knees to drink water
Brought their own swords and shields to camp
Were under twenty years of age
explanation: God instructed Gideon to test the men at the water; only the 300 who lapped water bringing it to their mouths were chosen (Judges 7:4–7).

text: Samson's great physical strength was tied to his vow as a:
options: Nazirite, which required that no razor touch his head
High Priest of the order of Levi
Levite musician in the sanctuary
King of Judah
explanation: Samson was dedicated to God from the womb as a Nazirite, with the condition that his hair must never be cut (Judges 13:5; 16:17).

text: Hannah prayed fervently at the sanctuary in Shiloh for a child, promising God that if given a son, she would:
options: Dedicate him to the Lord's service all the days of his life as a Nazirite.
Offer one hundred bullocks at the temple.
Make him a king over Israel.
Fast for forty days every year.
explanation: 1 Samuel 1:11 records Hannah's vow that if God gave her a male child, she would give him to the Lord all his life, and no razor would touch his head.

text: Eli the priest was judged by God because he failed to:
options: Restrain his sons, Hophni and Phinehas, from their blasphemous and immoral conduct in the sanctuary.
Offer sacrifices on the Day of Atonement.
Anoint Saul as king over Israel.
Build a permanent temple in Jerusalem.
explanation: God revealed to young Samuel that judgment was coming upon Eli's house because his sons made themselves vile, and he did not restrain them (1 Samuel 2:22–36; 3:13).

text: When the young boy Samuel heard his name called three times in the night, Eli eventually realized it was God and advised him to respond:
options: Speak, Lord, for your servant hears.
Here I am, father Eli.
Lord, why have you called me?
Praise the Lord, O my soul.
explanation: 1 Samuel 3:8–9 shows Eli discerning that the Lord was calling the boy, instructing Samuel to answer, "Speak, Lord, for your servant hears."

text: Why did the Israelites demand a human king from Samuel at Ramah?
options: They wanted to be like all the surrounding nations and have a king to lead them into battle.
God explicitly commanded them to abolish the priesthood.
Samuel refused to judge them anymore.
The Philistines forced them to elect a monarch.
explanation: Israel rejected God's direct theocracy, asking Samuel for a king because Samuel was old and his sons were corrupt (1 Samuel 8:4–20).

text: Who was anointed by Samuel as the first king of Israel?
options: Saul, son of Kish
David, son of Jesse
Abner, son of Ner
Jonathan, son of Saul
explanation: Samuel anointed Saul, a Benjaminite, as the first earthly king over Israel after God selected him (1 Samuel 9–10).

text: King Saul was rejected by God from being king over Israel primarily because he:
options: Disobeyed God's command regarding the complete destruction of the Amalekites and offered unauthorized sacrifices.
Refused to fight against Goliath the Philistine.
Built idols in Dan and Bethel.
Taxed the people too heavily.
explanation: Saul spared King Agag and the best livestock against God's instruction (1 Samuel 15), leading Samuel to declare: "To obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22).

text: Samuel anointed David as king at Bethlehem while Saul was still reigning because:
options: God had rejected Saul and directed Samuel to the house of Jesse.
Jesse demanded that one of his sons be crowned.
David had defeated the Amalekites in battle.
The elders of Judah elected David secretly.
explanation: God told Samuel not to look on physical appearance, stating that man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart (1 Samuel 16:1–13).

text: David defeated the Philistine giant Goliath using:
options: A sling and a single smooth stone, coming in the name of the Lord of Hosts.
King Saul's heavy armor and broadsword.
A surprise night attack with 300 soldiers.
A spear borrowed from his brother Eliab.
explanation: David rejected Saul's armor, confronting Goliath with his staff, sling, five smooth stones, and faith in the God of Israel (1 Samuel 17:40–50).

text: The covenant of deep friendship made between David and Saul's son Jonathan was demonstrated when Jonathan:
options: Warned David of Saul's plans to kill him and gave David his robe, armor, and bow.
Helped David conquer the city of Jebus.
Left his father's house to live with David in the wilderness.
Crowned David as king in Gibeah.
explanation: Jonathan loved David as his own soul, stripping himself of his royal robe and armor to give them to David, and protecting him from Saul (1 Samuel 18:1–4; 20).

text: David committed a grave sin against God when he took Bathsheba and arranged the death of her husband:
options: Uriah the Hittite
Joab the commander
Abner the general
Ahimelech the priest
explanation: David committed adultery with Bathsheba and ordered Uriah to be placed on the front lines of battle where he would be killed (2 Samuel 11).

text: Which prophet confronted King David about his sin with Bathsheba using the parable of the rich man and the poor man's ewe lamb?
options: Nathan
Gad
Samuel
Ahijah
explanation: Nathan told David the parable of the stolen ewe lamb, declaring "You are the man!" which brought David to deep repentance (2 Samuel 12:1–13; Psalm 51).

text: When God asked King Solomon in a dream at Gibeon what he desired, Solomon asked for:
options: An understanding heart (wisdom) to govern God's people and discern between good and evil.
Great wealth and long life.
The destruction of all his political enemies.
Victory in military conquests across Asia.
explanation: Solomon asked for wisdom to lead Israel, pleasing God, who granted him wisdom along with unasked riches and honor (1 Kings 3:5–14).

text: Solomon demonstrated his great wisdom publicly when resolving a dispute between two mothers by:
options: Proposing to divide a living baby in two with a sword, which revealed the true mother through her compassion.
Consulting the High Priest's Urim and Thummim.
Casting lots before the elders.
Ordering both women to be imprisoned until one confessed.
explanation: The genuine mother pleaded for the child's life to be spared, giving him to the other woman, which proved her true maternity to Solomon (1 Kings 3:16–28).

text: Solomon's spiritual downfall in his later years was caused primarily by:
options: Marrying many foreign wives who turned his heart away after foreign gods.
Ceasing the daily morning sacrifices in the temple.
Trying to invade the kingdom of Assyria.
Demolishing the temple he built in Jerusalem.
explanation: 1 Kings 11:1–8 notes that Solomon loved many foreign women who led him to build high places for false gods like Chemosh and Molech, provoking God's anger.

text: The Kingdom of Israel split into two after the death of Solomon because his son Rehoboam:
options: Rejected the advice of the elders and increased the labor burden and taxation on the northern tribes.
Was defeated in war by Jeroboam.
Moved the national capital from Jerusalem to Samaria.
Abolished the priesthood of Levi.
explanation: Rehoboam followed his young peers' advice, telling the people his little finger would be thicker than his father's waist, causing ten northern tribes to rebel under Jeroboam (1 Kings 12).

text: After the kingdom divided, Jeroboam I instituted false worship in the Northern Kingdom of Israel by setting up two golden calves at:
options: Bethel and Dan
Shechem and Penuel
Samaria and Jezreel
Shiloh and Gilgal
explanation: To prevent northern Israelites from traveling to Jerusalem to worship, Jeroboam set up golden calves in Dan and Bethel, leading Israel into continuous sin (1 Kings 12:26–33).

text: Prophet Elijah declared a multi-year drought upon Israel during the reign of King Ahab as judgment for:
options: Promoting Baal worship introduced by his Phoenician wife, Jezebel.
Refusing to build city walls around Samaria.
Forming a military alliance with the King of Syria.
Selling the temple treasures to foreign merchants.
explanation: Ahab did more evil than all who were before him, marrying Jezebel and serving Baal. Elijah confronted him by declaring there would be no rain except by his word (1 Kings 16:30–33; 17:1).

text: During the contest on Mount Carmel between Elijah and the 450 prophets of Baal, God proved He was the true God by:
options: Answering Elijah's prayer with fire from heaven that consumed the sacrifice, wood, stones, and water.
Causing an immediate earthquake that swallowed the prophets of Baal.
Striking King Ahab with leprosy instantly.
Sending a swarm of locusts on the altar of Baal.
explanation: When Elijah prayed, the fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt offering, leading the people to shout, "The Lord, He is God!" (1 Kings 18:36–39).

text: How did King Ahab and Queen Jezebel illegally acquire Naboth's vineyard?
options: Jezebel arranged false charges of blasphemy against Naboth, leading to his execution by stoning.
Ahab offered Naboth ten times the market price in gold.
Ahab seized it using the royal guard after a court decree.
Naboth sold it voluntarily to pay his debts.
explanation: When Naboth refused to sell his ancestral inheritance, Jezebel set up scoundrels to falsely accuse Naboth of cursing God and the king, causing him to be stoned (1 Kings 21).

text: Elisha received a double portion of Elijah's prophetic spirit because he:
options: Faithfully accompanied Elijah from Gilgal to Bethel, Jericho, and the Jordan, and witnessed Elijah being taken up to heaven in a whirlwind.
Defeated the Syrian army single-handedly.
Was the oldest son of a high priest.
Fasted for forty days in the wilderness of Damascus.
explanation: Elisha refused to leave Elijah's side. Elijah promised that if Elisha saw him when he was taken, the double portion would be his (2 Kings 2:1–15).

text: Naaman, the Syrian army commander, was cured of his leprosy by Prophet Elisha when he:
options: Dipped seven times in the Jordan River as instructed by Elisha's messenger.
Offered silver and golden garments at the altar in Samaria.
Was touched on his forehead by Elisha in person.
Prayed at the temple in Jerusalem for seven days.
explanation: Though initially angry at the simple command, Naaman obeyed his servants, dipped seven times in the Jordan River, and his skin was completely restored (2 Kings 5:1–14).

text: The central message of the prophet Amos to the Northern Kingdom of Israel focused on:
options: Divine justice, righteousness, and condemnation of social oppression of the poor.
Encouraging the people to rebuild the temple walls.
Predicting immediate victory over the Babylonians.
Promoting animal sacrifice rituals over ethical living.
explanation: Amos condemned Israel's empty religious rituals paired with social injustice, famously declaring: "Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream" (Amos 5:24).

text: Prophet Hosea's marriage to Gomer, an unfaithful wife, symbolized:
options: God's persistent love and willingness to redeem unfaithful Israel despite her spiritual adultery (idolatry).
The legal process of divorce under the Mosaic Law.
The social customs of the Philistines.
The personal tragedy of all Old Testament prophets.
explanation: Hosea's painful marriage reflected God's relationship with Israel, showing how Israel turned to false gods while God continually sought her restoration (Hosea 1–3).

text: King Josiah of Judah initiated sweeping religious reforms throughout the land after:
options: Hilkiah the High Priest discovered the Book of the Law in the temple during repairs.
An army of angels defeated the Assyrians outside Jerusalem.
He visited the ruins of the northern kingdom in Samaria.
Prophet Isaiah brought him a letter from God.
explanation: Upon hearing the words of the newly found Book of the Law, Josiah tore his clothes in repentance and cleansed Judah of all idolatrous shrines and altars (2 Kings 22–23).

text: Prophet Jeremiah is often called the "Weeping Prophet" because he:
options: Grieved deeply over the persistent sins of Judah and the impending destruction of Jerusalem by Babylon.
Lost his entire family during a famine in Anathoth.
Was blind from birth.
Was exiled to Assyria in chains.
explanation: Jeremiah mourned over his nation's stubborn idolatry and the judgment of the Babylonian captivity, as expressed throughout Jeremiah and Lamentations.

text: Jeremiah prophesied about a "New Covenant" (Jeremiah 31:31–34) which differed from the Sinai covenant because God would:
options: Write His law directly upon their hearts and minds, offering full forgiveness of sins.
Require twice as many animal sacrifices.
Restrict salvation exclusively to the tribe of Judah.
Establish an earthly empire ruled from Babylon.
explanation: Jeremiah foresaw an internal, spiritual covenant fulfilled in Christ, where God's law is written on human hearts rather than stone tablets (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Hebrews 8:8–12).

text: According to Luke Chapter 1, the Angel Gabriel announced the birth of Jesus to the Virgin Mary in the city of:
options: Nazareth
Bethlehem
Jerusalem
Capernaum
explanation: The Angel Gabriel was sent by God to Nazareth, a city of Galilee, to a virgin betrothed to Joseph named Mary (Luke 1:26–27).

text: Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea primarily because:
options: Joseph and Mary traveled there to be registered in a census ordered by Caesar Augustus.
Joseph owned a permanent residential estate in Bethlehem.
The Jerusalem temple was closed for repairs.
An angel instructed them to move there permanently.
explanation: Caesar Augustus issued a decree for a worldwide census, requiring Joseph to go to his ancestral city, Bethlehem (the city of David), with Mary (Luke 2:1–7; Micah 5:2).

text: When the infant Jesus was presented in the Temple at Jerusalem, which righteous devout man recognized Him as the Lord's Christ and praised God?
options: Simeon
Nicodemus
Caiaphas
Gamaliel
explanation: Simeon had been promised by the Holy Spirit that he would not die before seeing the Messiah. He took Jesus in his arms and prayed the Nunc Dimittis (Luke 2:25–35).

text: John the Baptist conducted his ministry of preaching repentance and baptizing people in the:
options: Jordan River
Sea of Galilee
Pool of Siloam
Dead Sea
explanation: Matthew 3:1–6 records John preaching in the wilderness of Judea and baptizing confessing believers in the Jordan River.

text: During the baptism of Jesus by John, what divine confirmation occurred as Jesus came out of the water?
options: The heavens opened, the Holy Spirit descended like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, This is my beloved Son.
A pillar of fire appeared over the water.
An angel placed a gold crown on Jesus' head.
The Jordan River dried up temporarily.
explanation: All three Gospel synoptics record the Spirit descending like a dove and the Father's voice testifying to Jesus' sonship at His baptism (Matthew 3:16–17).

text: When Satan tempted Jesus in the wilderness to turn stones into bread after forty days of fasting, Jesus resisted by quoting scripture:
options: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart.
The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want.
Do not cast your pearls before swine.
explanation: Jesus quoted Deuteronomy 8:3 to overcome the physical temptation of hunger, setting an example of using the Word of God as spiritual truth (Matthew 4:4).

text: In the Sermon on the Mount, the beatitude "Blessed are the peacemakers" is followed by which promise?
options: For they shall be called sons of God.
For they shall inherit the earth.
For theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
For they shall obtain mercy.
explanation: Matthew 5:9 reads: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God."

text: What was Jesus' first recorded miracle in the Gospel of John?
options: Turning water into wine at the wedding feast in Cana of Galilee
Healing the nobleman's son
Calming the storm on the lake
Raising Lazarus from the dead
explanation: John 2:1–11 identifies the transformation of water into wine at Cana as the first of Jesus' miraculous signs, manifesting His glory.

text: When four men brought a paralytic man to Jesus by lowering his bed through the roof, Jesus first said to the paralytic:
options: Son, your sins are forgiven.
Take up your bed and walk immediately.
Do you believe I can heal you?
Go and show yourself to the priest.
explanation: Seeing their faith, Jesus first addressed the man's spiritual need by forgiving his sins, before healing his paralysis to prove His authority on earth (Mark 2:1–12).

text: In the parable of the Sower (Matthew 13), the seed that fell on good soil represents:
options: The person who hears the word of God, understands it, and bears abundant fruit.
People who hear the word but let worldly worries choke it.
Those who receive the word with joy but fall away during persecution.
Those who reject the word outright.
explanation: Jesus explained that good soil represents an open, receptive heart that understands the Gospel message and yields spiritual fruit (Matthew 13:23).

text: Jesus taught in the parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10) that a person's "neighbor" is:
options: Anyone in need to whom we show love and mercy, regardless of racial or religious barriers.
Only people who live in the same neighborhood.
Fellow members of the same religious group.
Those who perform good deeds in return.
explanation: The Samaritan helped the beaten Jew when the priest and Levite passed by, teaching that true neighborliness means extending mercy to anyone in need (Luke 10:25–37).

text: The central lesson of the parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15) is:
options: God's boundless grace, love, and joy in forgiving repentant sinners.
How younger sons should manage their financial inheritances.
The importance of strict agricultural labor rules.
That older brothers are always right.
explanation: The father running to welcome his returning son illustrates God's eager forgiveness for every sinner who repents (Luke 15:11–32).

text: Who was the tax collector in Jericho who climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus and pledged to give half his goods to the poor?
options: Zacchaeus
Matthew
Levi
Cornelius
explanation: Luke 19:1–10 records Zacchaeus climbing the tree. Upon receiving Jesus in his house, he repented and offered restitution, prompting Jesus to declare that salvation had come to his house.

text: At Caesarea Philippi, when Jesus asked His disciples "Who do you say that I am?", Peter answered:
options: You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.
You are Elijah or one of the ancient prophets.
You are John the Baptist resurrected.
You are the King of Israel who will defeat Rome.
explanation: Peter made this confession of faith under divine revelation, upon which Jesus declared He would build His Church (Matthew 16:13–18).

text: Which Old Testament figures appeared in glory conversing with Jesus during His Transfiguration on the mountain?
options: Moses and Elijah
Abraham and Isaac
David and Solomon
Enoch and Noah
explanation: Moses (representing the Law) and Elijah (representing the Prophets) appeared with Jesus on the Mount of Transfiguration, speaking of His upcoming departure in Jerusalem (Matthew 17:1–8; Luke 9:28–36).

text: During the Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem, Jesus rode on a colt (donkey) to fulfill the prophecy of:
options: Zechariah 9:9
Isaiah 53:1
Psalm 22:1
Malachi 3:1
explanation: Matthew 21:4–5 notes that Jesus rode a colt to fulfill Zechariah 9:9: "Behold, your King is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey."

text: Jesus cleansed the Temple in Jerusalem by driving out money changers and merchants, declaring:
options: My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves.
The Temple will be destroyed in three days.
Tithe your mint and cumin before entering.
Only priests are permitted in these courts.
explanation: Quoting Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11, Jesus overturned the tables of those who commercialized the outer courts of God's house (Matthew 21:12–13).

text: During the Last Supper, Jesus instituted the Lord's Supper (Eucharist), giving bread and wine to His disciples as symbols of His:
options: Body broken and Blood shed for the forgiveness of sins
Victory over the Roman Empire
Miraculous feeding of the five thousand
Power to perform future healings
explanation: Jesus broke bread ("This is my body") and passed the cup ("This is my blood of the new covenant"), establishing the memorial feast for His believers (Matthew 26:26–28; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26).

text: Where did Jesus experience deep agony in prayer, sweating like drops of blood, while submitting to the Father's will before His arrest?
options: The Garden of Gethsemane
The Mount of Olives peak
The upper room in Jerusalem
The wilderness of Judea
explanation: At Gethsemane, Jesus prayed, "Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me; nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done" (Luke 22:39–44).

text: Which disciple betrayed Jesus to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver with a kiss?
options: Judas Iscariot
Simon Peter
Thomas Didymus
Philip
explanation: Judas Iscariot agreed to hand Jesus over for thirty silver pieces, identifying Him in Gethsemane with a kiss (Matthew 26:14–16, 47–50).

text: Before the Roman governor Pontius Pilate, Jesus was first tried by the Jewish supreme council known as the:
options: Sanhedrin
Pharisees Assembly
Essene Council
Zealot Brotherhood
explanation: Following His arrest, Jesus was brought before the High Priest Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin council, who found Him guilty of blasphemy (Matthew 26:57–66).

text: How many times did Simon Peter deny knowing Jesus before the rooster crowed, as foretold by Jesus?
options: Three times
Two times
Four times
Seven times
explanation: While warming himself in the High Priest's courtyard, Peter denied knowing Jesus three times. Immediately, the rooster crowed, and Peter wept bitterly (Luke 22:54–62).

text: What criminal did the crowd demand Pontius Pilate release instead of Jesus during the Passover custom?
options: Barabbas
Simon of Cyrene
Dismas
Alexander
explanation: Though Pilate found no guilt in Jesus, the crowd, stirred up by the chief priests, demanded the release of Barabbas, a murderer and rebel (Matthew 27:15–26).

text: Who was forced by Roman soldiers to carry the cross of Jesus on the way to Golgotha?
options: Simon of Cyrene
Joseph of Arimathea
John the Apostle
Nicodemus
explanation: As Jesus was led away, the soldiers compelled Simon, a man from Cyrene in North Africa, to carry Jesus' cross behind Him (Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26).

text: The place where Jesus was crucified was called Golgotha, which means:
options: Place of a Skull
Hill of Olives
Mount of Blessing
Valley of Decision
explanation: Mark 15:22 and John 19:17 explain that Golgotha translates to "the Place of a Skull" (Calvary in Latin).

text: What cry of agony did Jesus utter from the cross around the ninth hour, according to Matthew 27:46?
options: Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani? (My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?)
Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.
It is finished.
Into your hands I commit my spirit.
explanation: Jesus quoted Psalm 22:1 on the cross, expressing the deep agony of bearing the sin of humanity (Matthew 27:46).

text: What significant event occurred in the Jerusalem Temple at the moment Jesus died?
options: The curtain (veil) of the Temple was torn in two from top to bottom.
The Ark of the Covenant vanished.
The altar of burnt offering cracked in half.
The golden lampstand was extinguished.
explanation: The tearing of the Temple veil symbolized that direct access to God was now open to all people through the sacrifice of Jesus (Matthew 27:51; Hebrews 10:19–20).

text: Who provided the tomb in which Jesus was buried after His crucifixion?
options: Joseph of Arimathea
Nicodemus
Lazarus of Bethany
Simon the Leper
explanation: Joseph of Arimathea, a wealthy member of the council and secret disciple, asked Pilate for Jesus' body and placed it in his own unused rock-hewn tomb (Matthew 27:57–60).

text: Who were the first witnesses to discover the empty tomb on the first day of the week?
options: Mary Magdalene and other faithful women
Peter and John
The Roman guards on duty
Cleopas and his companion
explanation: Early on Sunday morning, Mary Magdalene and other women went to the tomb to anoint Jesus' body and found the stone rolled away and angels declaring He was risen (Matthew 28:1–8; John 20:1–2).

text: On the day of His resurrection, Jesus walked alongside two disciples traveling to a village named:
options: Emmaus
Jericho
Bethany
Joppa
explanation: Luke 24:13–35 describes Jesus joining two downcast disciples on the seven-mile road to Emmaus, opening the Scriptures to them regarding the Messiah.

text: When did the two disciples on the road to Emmaus finally recognize that their companion was the risen Jesus?
options: When He took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them.
When He showed them His hands and feet.
As soon as He began speaking to them on the road.
When He performed a healing in their home.
explanation: Luke 24:30–31 notes that as Jesus broke bread at the table, their eyes were opened, they recognized Him, and He vanished from their sight.

text: Which disciple refused to believe that Jesus had risen until he could see and touch the nail marks in His hands and side?
options: Thomas
Andrew
Bartholomew
James
explanation: Thomas doubted the other disciples' testimonies until Jesus appeared eight days later, inviting Thomas to touch His hands and side, prompting Thomas to proclaim, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:24–29).

text: At the Sea of Tiberias (Galilee), how did the risen Jesus restore Simon Peter after his three denials?
options: By asking him three times, Do you love me? and commanding him, Feed my sheep.
By rebuking him in front of all the apostles.
By requiring him to fast for forty days.
By re-baptizing him in the sea.
explanation: Jesus asked Peter three times if he loved Him, mirroring Peter's three denials and recommissioning him to care for His flock (John 21:15–19).

text: Before His Ascension, Jesus gave His disciples the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19–20), instructing them to:
options: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to obey His commands.
Stay in Jerusalem and establish a political government.
Build physical church structures across Judea.
Write books summarizing Old Testament laws.
explanation: The Great Commission commands believers to spread the Gospel worldwide, make disciples, baptize them, and teach Christ's doctrines (Matthew 28:18–20).

text: Where did Jesus ascend into heaven forty days after His resurrection?
options: Mount of Olives (near Bethany)
Mount Sinai
Mount Carmel
Mount Hermon
explanation: Luke 24:50–51 and Acts 1:9–12 record Jesus leading His disciples out as far as Bethany on the Mount of Olives, where He blessed them and was taken up into heaven.

text: What command did Jesus give to His apostles right before His Ascension regarding their waiting period in Jerusalem?
options: Do not leave Jerusalem, but wait for the gift my Father promised (the Holy Spirit).
Flee immediately to Galilee to escape persecution.
Elect a new king over Israel before preaching.
Travel immediately to Rome to preach to Caesar.
explanation: Acts 1:4–5 records Jesus telling the apostles to wait in Jerusalem until they received the baptism of the Holy Spirit for power.

text: Two men in white clothing (angels) assured the apostles after Jesus ascended that:
options: This same Jesus, who was taken into heaven, will come back in the same way they saw Him go.
Jesus would return within three days.
They should build a monument on top of the mountain.
They should stop preaching in public places.
explanation: Acts 1:10–11 records the angels promising the visible, physical second coming of Jesus Christ.

text: Who was chosen by lot to replace Judas Iscariot as the twelfth apostle in Acts Chapter 1?
options: Matthias
Barnabas
Barsabbas (Justus)
Stephen
explanation: The early church prayed and cast lots between Joseph called Barsabbas and Matthias; the lot fell to Matthias, numbering him with the eleven apostles (Acts 1:21–26).

text: Which prophet's Old Testament prophecy did Peter quote on the Day of Pentecost to explain the outpouring of the Holy Spirit?
options: Joel
Malachi
Micah
Habakkuk
explanation: In Acts 2:16–21, Peter explained the Pentecost phenomenon by quoting Joel 2:28–32 ("In the last days, God says, I will pour out my Spirit on all people").

text: How many people repented, were baptized, and were added to the Church following Peter's sermon on the Day of Pentecost?
options: About three thousand
About five hundred
About twelve thousand
Exactly one hundred and twenty
explanation: Acts 2:41 records that those who accepted Peter's message were baptized, adding about three thousand souls to the early fellowship that day.

text: The prominent feature of community life among the early believers in Jerusalem (Acts 2:44–45; 4:32–35) was that:
options: They held all things in common, sharing possessions so no one among them was in need.
They lived in isolation in the Judean desert.
They collected taxes for the Roman authorities.
They established private commercial banks.
explanation: Believers demonstrated love by selling property and distributing proceeds to anyone in need, living in deep unity and fellowship.

text: Why were Ananias and his wife Sapphira struck dead by God in Acts Chapter 5?
options: They lied to the Holy Spirit by holding back part of the proceeds while pretending to give everything.
They refused to pay taxes to Rome.
They worshipped idols in secret.
They physically attacked Peter and John.
explanation: Peter revealed that Ananias and Sapphira had lied not merely to men, but to God the Holy Spirit by keeping back money deceptively (Acts 5:1–11).

text: Seven men full of the Spirit and wisdom, including Stephen and Philip, were originally appointed in Acts Chapter 6 to:
options: Oversee the daily distribution of food to Hellenistic (Greek-speaking) widows.
Lead military defenses for Jerusalem.
Replace the Sanhedrin judges.
Collect Temple tithes.
explanation: To resolve a dispute over neglected Hellenistic widows, the apostles instructed the church to select seven deacons to handle food distribution so the apostles could focus on prayer and preaching (Acts 6:1–6).

text: Who became the first Christian martyr after testifying boldly before the Sanhedrin?
options: Stephen
James, the son of Zebedee
Philip
Barnabas
explanation: Stephen was stoned to death after proclaiming the Gospel to the council. As he died, he prayed for his executioners' forgiveness (Acts 6:8–15; 7:54–60).

text: Which young Pharisee approved of Stephen's execution and guarded the robes of those who stoned him?
options: Saul of Tarsus (later Paul)
Gamaliel
Alexander
Tertullus
explanation: Acts 7:58 and 8:1 state that the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul, who approved of Stephen's death.

text: Philip the Evangelist preached the Gospel in Samaria and was later led by the Spirit to explain Isaiah 53 to an official from:
options: Ethiopia (the treasurer of Candace)
Egypt
Rome
Damascus
explanation: Philip met the Ethiopian eunuch on the road to Gaza, led him to faith in Christ using Isaiah 53, and baptized him in nearby water (Acts 8:26–39).

text: Saul was dramatically converted on the road to Damascus when:
options: A bright light from heaven flashed around him and Jesus spoke to him, asking, Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?
An angel appeared to him in a dream.
He read a letter written by Peter.
He heard the preaching of Barnabas in the synagogue.
explanation: A heavenly light struck Saul blind, and Jesus identified Himself, transforming Saul from a persecutor into an apostle (Acts 9:1–19; 22:6–16).

text: Who was sent by God in Damascus to lay hands on Saul so that he might regain his sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit?
options: Ananias of Damascus
Cornelius
Silas
Agabus
explanation: Despite initial fear of Saul's reputation, Ananias obeyed God's vision, prayed for Saul, restored his sight, and baptized him (Acts 9:10–19).

text: At Joppa, Peter raised from the dead a faithful female disciple known for her good works and charity toward widows named:
options: Tabitha (Dorcas)
Lydia
Rhoda
Priscilla
explanation: Tabitha (Dorcas) died in Joppa; Peter arrived, prayed, and commanded her to arise, causing many in Joppa to believe in the Lord (Acts 9:36–42).

text: Peter was taught through a heavenly vision of a sheet containing clean and unclean animals that:
options: God shows no favoritism, and no human being or Gentile should be called unclean or unacceptable to God.
Believers must strictly keep the Mosaic dietary laws.
He should move permanently to Caesarea.
Animal sacrifices were still required in the Temple.
explanation: The vision prepared Peter to go to the house of Cornelius, a Gentile, preaching salvation without requiring Judaic ceremonial ritual (Acts 10:9–35).

text: The Roman centurion in Caesarea who received Peter into his house and became the first Gentile convert along with his household was:
options: Cornelius
Julius
Sergius Paulus
Claudius Lysias
explanation: Cornelius was a God-fearing centurion whose family received the Holy Spirit while Peter was preaching, confirming Gentile inclusion in the Church (Acts 10:44–48).

text: In which city were the disciples of Jesus first called "Christians"?
options: Antioch (in Syria)
Jerusalem
Rome
Corinth
explanation: Acts 11:26 notes that Barnabas and Saul taught a large assembly in Antioch for a full year, where believers were first given the name "Christians."

text: Which apostle was executed with the sword by King Herod Agrippa I in Acts Chapter 12?
options: James, the brother of John
Peter
Andrew
Philip
explanation: Herod Agrippa I launched a persecution against the church, killing James the son of Zebedee with the sword and subsequently arresting Peter (Acts 12:1–2).

text: How was Peter miraculously delivered from Herod's heavily guarded prison in Jerusalem?
options: An angel of the Lord struck off his chains, opened the iron gate, and led him out safely.
Believers bought his freedom from the prison warden.
A sudden earthquake collapsed the prison walls.
Roman soldiers revolted against Herod.
explanation: While the church prayed fervently, an angel appeared in Peter's cell, loosened his chains, and guided him past two guard posts into the city (Acts 12:3–11).

text: Who accompanied Paul on his first missionary journey after being set apart by the Holy Spirit at Antioch?
options: Barnabas (and initially John Mark)
Silas and Timothy
Luke and Titus
Apollos and Aquila
explanation: Acts 13:1–3 records the Holy Spirit commissioning Barnabas and Saul for missionary work, taking John Mark as their helper.

text: The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15) met to address the crucial controversy of whether:
options: Gentile believers had to be circumcised and required to keep the Law of Moses to be saved.
Christians could pay taxes to the Roman Emperor.
Female believers could be appointed as apostles.
Paul should continue his journeys to Europe.
explanation: Certain Pharisaic believers argued that Gentiles needed circumcision. The council ruled that salvation is through the grace of the Lord Jesus alone (Acts 15:1–21).

text: What four specific guidelines did the Jerusalem Council send to Gentile churches to abstain from?
options: Food offered to idols, blood, meat of strangled animals, and sexual immorality.
Tithing, keeping the Sabbath, eating pork, and wearing wool.
Public prayer, singing hymns, drinking wine, and trading.
Fasting, traveling on Sunday, marrying unbelievers, and swearing oaths.
explanation: James and the apostles wrote a letter instructing Gentiles to avoid these four specific practices to maintain fellowship and holiness (Acts 15:28–29).

text: Why did Paul and Barnabas part ways before starting their second missionary journey?
options: They disagreed over taking John Mark with them, as Mark had previously departed from them in Pamphylia.
Barnabas wanted to return permanently to Jerusalem.
Paul wanted to preach exclusively to Jewish synagogues.
They had a dispute over church finances.
explanation: A sharp disagreement arose: Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas and traveled through Syria and Cilicia (Acts 15:36–41).

text: Paul crossed over to Europe (Macedonia) during his second journey after receiving a vision of:
options: A man of Macedonia standing and begging him, Come over to Macedonia and help us.
An angel placing a crown on his head.
A burning bush on top of a mountain.
A lion standing near the Aegean Sea.
explanation: The "Macedonian Call" guided Paul to bring the Gospel into Europe, starting at Philippi (Acts 16:9–10).

text: Who was Paul's first convert in Philippi, a businesswoman who sold purple fabric and opened her home to the mission team?
options: Lydia
Priscilla
Phoebe
Chloe
explanation: Lydia of Thyatira heard Paul's message, the Lord opened her heart, and she was baptized along with her household (Acts 16:14–15).

text: When Paul and Silas were imprisoned and chained at midnight in Philippi, what were they doing when an earthquake shook the prison foundations?
options: Praying and singing hymns to God
Trying to break their chains
Sleeping soundly
Planning an escape route
explanation: At midnight, Paul and Silas prayed and sang praises, leading to an earthquake that opened the doors and unfastened their bonds (Acts 16:25–26).

text: What question did the Philippian jailer ask Paul and Silas after seeing the prison doors opened, and what was their answer?
options: What must I do to be saved? - Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.
How did you open the doors? - By the power of Moses.
Will you escape now? - We are Roman citizens.
Who is your God? - The God of Abraham.
explanation: Prevented from committing suicide, the jailer fell down before Paul and Silas and received the Gospel message along with his family (Acts 16:27–34).

text: The believers in Berea (Acts 17:11) were praised as being more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica because they:
options: Received the word with great eagerness and examined the Scriptures daily to see if Paul's teachings were true.
Built a large worship center for Paul.
Donated large sums of money to the Jerusalem poor.
Protected Paul from Roman soldiers.
explanation: The Bereans tested every sermon against the OT Scriptures daily to verify the truth of Paul's gospel (Acts 17:10–12).

text: Where in Athens did Paul deliver his famous address regarding the altar dedicated to "THE UNKNOWN GOD"?
options: The Areopagus (Mars' Hill)
The Parthenon
The Temple of Zeus
The Roman Forum
explanation: Paul stood in the middle of the Areopagus, using their statue to "The Unknown God" as a bridge to declare the Creator God who resurrected Jesus (Acts 17:22–31).

text: Which Christian couple in Corinth worked as tentmakers alongside Paul and later instructed Apollos in the faith?
options: Priscilla and Aquila
Ananias and Sapphira
Philemon and Apphia
Felix and Drusilla
explanation: Paul stayed and worked with Priscilla and Aquila because they shared the trade of tentmaking. Later, they explained the way of God more accurately to Apollos at Ephesus (Acts 18:1–3, 24–26).

text: In Romans 3:23–24, Paul states that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, but believers are justified freely by:
options: God's grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.
Perfect observance of the Mosaic Law.
Offering annual blood sacrifices.
Performing good works in the community.
explanation: Justification is a free gift of God's grace received through faith in the atonement provided by Christ (Romans 3:21–26; 5:1).

text: According to Romans 6:23, what is the wages of sin, and what is the gift of God?
options: The wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
The wages of sin is poverty, but the gift of God is earthly wealth.
The wages of sin is fear, but the gift of God is human wisdom.
The wages of sin is exile, but the gift of God is political power.
explanation: Romans 6:23 contrasts spiritual and eternal death earned through sin with the free gift of eternal life through faith in Christ.

text: In 1 Corinthians Chapter 13 (the "Love Chapter"), Paul concludes that among faith, hope, and love, the greatest of these is:
options: Love
Faith
Hope
Prophecy
explanation: 1 Corinthians 13:13 states: "And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love. But the greatest of these is love."

text: In Galatians 5:22–23, which of the following is listed as part of the fruit of the Holy Spirit?
options: Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
Wisdom, wealth, long life, and victory over physical enemies.
Speaking in tongues, prophecy, miracles, and interpretation.
Fasting, tithing, keeping laws, and offering incense.
explanation: Paul contrasts the works of the flesh with the ninefold character produced by the Holy Spirit in a believer's life (Galatians 5:19–23).

text: In Ephesians 6:10–18, what weapon represents the "Sword of the Spirit" in the Christian spiritual armor?
options: The Word of God
The Shield of Faith
The Breastplate of Righteousness
The Belt of Truth
explanation: Ephesians 6:17 explicitly defines the offensive spiritual weapon: "Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God."

text: In Philippians 4:6, Paul instructs believers regarding anxiety to:
options: Be anxious for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let requests be made known to God.
Avoid all public gatherings during times of trouble.
Rely solely on personal human strength and effort.
Fast continuously until feelings of fear pass away.
explanation: Paul teaches that prayer combined with thanksgiving brings God's peace that surpasses understanding to guard hearts and minds (Philippians 4:6–7).

text: Paul wrote a personal letter to Philemon asking him to forgive and welcome back his runaway slave who had become a Christian, named:
options: Onesimus
Tychicus
Epaphroditus
Demas
explanation: Paul urged Philemon to receive Onesimus no longer as a mere bondservant, but as a beloved brother in Christ (Philemon 1:10–17).

text: In 2 Timothy 3:16–17, Paul writes that all Scripture is given by inspiration of God and is profitable for:
options: Teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness.
Political debates and national legislation only.
Earning material prosperity in life.
Demonstrating superiority over earthly rulers.
explanation: God-breathed Scripture equips the believer fully for every good work through sound doctrine, correction, and spiritual instruction (2 Timothy 3:16–17).

text: According to James 2:14–26, faith without works (action) is:
options: Dead
Complete
Acceptable before God
Sufficient for salvation
explanation: James teaches that genuine saving faith naturally expresses itself in practical good deeds and compassionate action; without them, faith is dead and useless (James 2:17, 26).

text: What does James identify in James 3:1–12 as a small member of the body that is capable of causing vast damage like a spark setting a forest on fire?
options: The tongue
The hand
The eye
The foot
explanation: James highlights the power of speech, warning that an untamed tongue can corrupt the whole body and unleash destruction (James 3:5–6).

text: In 1 Peter 2:9, believers in Christ are collectively described as:
options: A chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, God's special possession.
Earthly soldiers fighting physical kingdoms.
A political faction within the Roman Empire.
High priests of the order of Aaron.
explanation: Peter applies these titles to the Church, highlighting its calling to proclaim the praises of God who called them out of darkness into light.

text: In 1 John 4:8 and 4:16, the apostle John gives a fundamental definition of God's nature by declaring that:
options: God is love
God is law
God is judgment
God is wind
explanation: 1 John 4:8 states: "Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love."

text: According to 1 John 1:9, if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to:
options: Forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Require animal sacrifices at the altar.
Expose our faults publicly to everyone.
Punish us with physical poverty.
explanation: True confession and repentance bring divine cleansing and restored fellowship through the blood of Jesus Christ (1 John 1:7–9).

text: In Revelation 1:8, the Lord God introduces Himself as the "Alpha and the Omega," which signifies that He is:
options: The Beginning and the End
The Ruler of Rome
The Angel of Death
The Judge of Israel only
explanation: Alpha and Omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing God's eternal nature, sovereignty, and completion of all creation (Revelation 1:8; 22:13).

text: In Revelation Chapter 21, John sees a vision of the new place of eternal dwelling for God's redeemed people called:
options: The New Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God
The Garden of Eden restored in Babylon
The Tabernacle of Shiloh
Mount Sinai
explanation: Revelation 21:1–4 depicts the New Jerusalem, where God will dwell with His people, wiping away every tear, with no more death, sorrow, or pain.

text: What civic duty toward government authorities does Paul mandate for Christians in Romans 13:1–7?
options: Be subject to governing authorities, pay taxes, give honor, and respect rulers because authority is instituted by God.
Rebel against non-Christian governments immediately.
Refuse to pay taxes to secular rulers.
Establish an earthly army to overthrow tyrants.
explanation: Paul explains that civil government is ordained by God to maintain order, punish wrongdoers, and protect society (Romans 13:1–7).

text: What did Jesus command concerning paying taxes to Caesar in Matthew 22:21?
options: Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's.
Do not pay taxes to pagan emperors.
Pay taxes only if the emperor is righteous.
Offer money to the priests instead of Caesar.
explanation: Showing a Roman coin, Jesus balanced civil duty (paying Roman taxes) with spiritual obligation (giving God full devotion).

text: In 1 Timothy 2:1–3, Paul urges that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for:
options: All people, especially kings and all those in high positions, that we may live peaceful and quiet lives.
Only Christian apostles and pastors.
The immediate overthrow of political enemies.
Wealthy church donors.
explanation: Praying for political leaders fosters societal peace and order, pleasing God who desires all people to be saved (1 Timothy 2:1–4).

text: According to 2 Thessalonians 3:10, what rule did Paul establish regarding work and laziness in the church?
options: If anyone is not willing to work, let him not eat.
The church must feed everyone regardless of effort.
Only leaders are required to labor.
Work is unnecessary because the Lord is coming immediately.
explanation: Paul condemned idleness, instructing believers to earn their own living responsibly and avoid becoming burdens on others (2 Thessalonians 3:6–12).

text: In Ephesians 5:22–25, Paul compares the marital relationship between husband and wife to the relationship between:
options: Christ and the Church
Moses and Israel
David and Jonathan
God and the angels
explanation: Paul teaches wives to submit to their husbands as to the Lord, and husbands to love their wives selflessly, as Christ loved the Church and gave Himself up for her (Ephesians 5:22–33).

text: According to Ephesians 6:1–3, children are commanded to obey their parents in the Lord because this is:
options: Right, and it is the first commandment with a promise of well-being and long life on earth.
A rule required only until age twelve.
A Levitical civil law for Jewish culture only.
Optional for baptized believers.
explanation: Paul quotes the Fifth Commandment (Exodus 20:12), highlighting that honoring parents carries the blessing of long life (Ephesians 6:1–3).

text: In 2 Corinthians 9:7, what kind of giver does God love?
options: A cheerful giver
A reluctant giver
A wealthy giver
A forced giver
explanation: Paul encourages voluntary, purposeful financial giving: "Each of you should give what you have decided in your heart to give, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Corinthians 9:7).

text: According to 1 Timothy 6:10, what is identified as a root of all kinds of evil?
options: The love of money
Money itself
Earthly poverty
Political power
explanation: Scripture specifies that the love of money (greed)—not money itself—leads people away from the faith and pierces them with many griefs (1 Timothy 6:10).

text: What standard of forgiveness did Jesus establish in the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:12, 14–15)?
options: God forgives our trespasses as we forgive those who trespass against us.
We are required to forgive others only if they apologize first.
Forgiveness is automatic regardless of how we treat others.
We should forgive our friends but hold grudges against enemies.
explanation: Jesus taught that receiving God's forgiveness requires an open, forgiving heart toward others (Matthew 6:14–15; 18:21–35).

text: In Matthew 5:13–16, Jesus describes His followers in the world as:
options: The salt of the earth and the light of the world
The rulers of nations and judges of the earth
The wealthy of the world and the wise of the age
The recluses of the wilderness and hermits of the desert
explanation: Believers preserve society from moral decay (salt) and illuminate truth through visible good works that glorify God (light) (Matthew 5:13–16).

text: According to Galatians 6:2, believers fulfill the law of Christ when they:
options: Bear one another's burdens
Keep all traditional rituals
Judge non-believers publicly
Accumulate wealth for church buildings
explanation: Galatians 6:2 states: "Carry each other's burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ" (the law of love).

text: In Hebrews 10:24–25, Christians are exhorted not to give up:
options: Meeting together (fellowship), but encouraging one another as the Day approaches.
Observance of Jewish fast days.
Daily temple sacrifices in Jerusalem.
Seeking personal administrative positions in government.
explanation: Corporate fellowship and mutual encouragement are vital for maintaining spiritual strength and perseverance in faith (Hebrews 10:24–25).

text: What primary test of true religion does James give in James 1:27?
options: To look after orphans and widows in their distress and to keep oneself unpolluted by the world.
To memorize all five books of the Law of Moses.
To fast twice a week and make long public prayers.
To build grand places of worship in every city.
explanation: Pure religion combines active, practical compassion for the vulnerable with personal moral holiness (James 1:27).

text: In 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18, what is God's explicit will for believers in Christ Jesus?
options: Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances.
Fast every week, isolate from unbelievers, seek earthly success.
Perform miracles daily, accumulate riches, build temples.
Avoid all political laws, live in isolation, stop working.

text: According to Revelation 22:14, who has the right to the tree of life and may enter through the gates into the heavenly city?
options: Those who wash their robes (cleanse themselves through the blood of the Lamb).

Those who were earthly kings and rulers.

explanation: Revelation 22:14 concludes with the promise that those purified by Christ have eternal access to the Tree of Life and eternal fellowship with God in the New Jerusalem.
